doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Transcribing Bird and Coltrane; how he thinks when improvising
summary: On All the Things You Are, his transcribing of alto heroes, and hearing lines ahead rather than chord by chord.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: When you’re playing on a tune like “All the Things You Are” —
Are you actually thinking, okay, I’m on G minor 7 to C 7. Are you thinking that or are you not thinking that?

That’s a very good question and I’ve mentioned this a few times to some students, and usually they don’t ask me but I’ll tell them — first of all when I was younger, and I’m a pretty good improviser, better than most at 16, there was a certain point where I started to become good, listening, transcribing. I have a whole loose leaf book of solos so I developed my ear which was so-so I think, listening to Charlie Parker, Coltrane. Even one bar, write it down. You know, Cannonball, you know, Sonny Stitt — Bird, Sonny Stitt around the same age, and Cannonball, next generation. On alto, Coltrane and Sonny Rollins. Those were my favorite. Not to negate Coleman Hawkins or Ben Webster and all those other people that are great. They didn’t have the excitement of the sixteenth notes and the more modern sound. So I went to those five people I just mentioned. Now when I listen back to old timers they sound beautiful. They’re all great. Desmond I didn’t listen to too much. He was totally innate. It was too light a sound for me. It wasn’t as exciting. Because you know, it’s just me. But as far as that goes, when I was younger, “All the Things You Are” I couldn’t play that tune too well on alto. I was playing piano too. For some reason the chord progression confused my mind. The first eight bars repeat in a different key and then the bridge is different and then it goes back to the first eight with a tag of four bars. When I play that tune now I’m being cocky when I say this, but I own that tune. There are certain tunes that I’ve played so much that, and I tell the students, I’m not thinking chord by chord anymore, on piano, even saxophone. I kind of see the chords. I know chords very well. But I’m hearing the whole line for four or eight bars when I play and I’m not playing the same thing all the time. But I just hear that. It’s like you

know the scene is coming up. Like if you’re in a boat and you’re going out to a destination, you know what you are seeing. You can see it, or imagine getting off the boat and walking in the sand and you reach the hotel or something. Whatever. I can kind of see that.
You can play or think a few measures ahead?
